summary:
Mississippi stands under the United States national framework on travel documents and entry, and that framework is the first exposure a trans visitor faces. Executive Order 14168 of January 2025 defined sex for federal purposes as a male-female binary and barred self-selection of gender on passports and visas; the State Department stopped processing the X marker and any marker not matching sex assigned at birth, so new passports are issued only as M or F on supporting documents, while passports already issued with an X marker remain valid until expiry. The Supreme Court allowed the passport sex-marker restrictions to take effect in November 2025. Trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, with some left stranded abroad; the ACLU is suing the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs.

Entry screening carries its own exposure. The State Department announced in February 2025 that it would flag visa applicants with an internal marking and treat as fraud, with a permanent bar, any applicant listing a gender other than the one assigned at birth, in connection with barring trans athletes from competing in women's sports in the United States. Separately, Transportation Security Administration checkpoint procedures involve secondary screening, hand-held devices and pat-downs that can be invasive of privacy and risk outing a trans traveller.

At state level, Mississippi has legislated against trans people across facilities, documents and care. A law signed 13 May 2024 and effective immediately requires individuals in public schools to use bathrooms consistent with sex "determined solely by birth"; the Movement Advancement Project's equality map records that Mississippi enacted bathroom and facilities bans in 2024 and 2025 and defines sex by birth in statute. A 2024 Harrison County dress code requiring clothing to match sex assigned at birth led to a transgender girl being threatened with in-school suspension for wearing a dress to a regional band event. In April 2025 two broader anti-trans bills, the SAFER Act and the Women's Bill of Rights, died in the legislature after lawmakers failed to agree on compromise versions by 29 April 2024, so the adult-facility and statutory sex-definition restrictions they would have imposed did not pass that session.

The Anti-Trans National Legal Risk Assessment Map's July 2026 update places Mississippi in its "Worst Laws Passed" category, among states the assessment describes as having legislatively erased transgender people; the grading derives from a five-year legislation-tracking methodology with a scoring rubric.

Identity documents are closed at state level. From 1 November 2021 to March 2026 a Gender Designation Form signed by a physician or psychotherapist allowed driver's licence marker changes, until a March 2026 law prohibited markers not reflecting sex assigned at birth. The Vital Records office issues an amended birth certificate with a new name and gender marker upon a certified court order, a medical statement attesting to gender reassignment and a fee, but lists both the updated and original information. On 17 April 2025 the Mississippi Supreme Court ruled 8-1 that a transgender teen undergoing gender transition could not change his name, denying a petition filed nearly two years earlier by a then-16-year-old whose parents both consented; the majority opinion by Justice James D. Maxwell II referred to the trans boy as a "minor female" and cited the 2023 REAP Act as Mississippi's express public policy against children receiving gender-transition assistance. A separate enacted measure prohibits inmate name changes.

Care for trans youth is banned. The Regulate Experimental Adolescent Procedures (REAP) Act, signed 28 February 2023, bans gender-affirming care for individuals under 18; after it took effect the University of Mississippi Medical Center's TEAM Clinic closed on 30 June 2023, leaving Spectrum: The Other Clinic in Hattiesburg operating virtually as the only LGBTQ+-specializing clinic in the state.

School sport is restricted. SB 2536, signed 11 March 2021 and effective 1 July 2021, bars transgender students from school sports consistent with their gender identity and requires any athlete whose sex is disputed to provide a physician's statement verifying genitalia, DNA and hormone levels.

Violence against trans women is documented. The U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of Mississippi reported that Joshua Brandon Vallum was sentenced to 49 years in federal prison for the bias-motivated murder of a transgender woman in Lucedale, a federal prosecution under the 2009 Matthew Shepard and James Byrd Jr. Act. A July 2026 state-by-state analysis of killings of trans women (per 100,000 trans women per year, 2008-2025, adjusted for undercounting) records 6.6 such killings per 100,000 annually for Mississippi, above the US general-population homicide rate of 6.0 per 100,000 printed as a comparison line; the analysis's headline finding is that law tiers do not sort violence, with both worst-law and safest-law states carrying high rates.

State non-discrimination law provides no protection based on gender identity in employment, housing or public accommodations, though federal Title VII per Bostock v. Clayton County (15 June 2020) prohibits employment discrimination based on gender identity. The 1994 state hate-crime statute does not include gender identity, though federal prosecution remains available under the 2009 Matthew Shepard and James Byrd Jr. Act. The Religious Liberty Accommodations Act (HB 1523) protects refusal of services based on belief that gender is determined at birth by anatomy and genetics.

Same-sex marriage has been recognized since 26 June 2015 under Obergefell v. Hodges, overriding Mississippi's 1996 executive order, 1997 statutory ban and 2004 constitutional Amendment 1, though those bans remain unrepealed. Mississippi's sodomy statute originating in 1839, with up to ten years' imprisonment, remains on the books unenforceable since Lawrence v. Texas (2003), and persons convicted before 2003 are still required to register as sex offenders under the 1995 registration law.
tangentialFactors:
Mississippi's legal-risk tier does not sort violence outcomes. The July 2026 killings analysis places Mississippi at 6.6 killings of trans women per 100,000 trans women per year (2008-2025, adjusted for undercounting), above the 6.0 per 100,000 US general-population homicide rate, and reports that both worst-law and safest-law states carry high rates, so a visitor should not read the state's "Worst Laws Passed" grading as either an explanation of or a protection from violence risk.

Local climate is uneven within the state. Starkville hosted its first pride parade on 24 March 2018 after an initial permit denial, drawing approximately 3,000 participants and becoming the largest parade in the city's history. Four cities, Jackson, Clarksdale, Holly Springs and Magnolia, ban gender-identity discrimination in employment, housing and public accommodations, while Hattiesburg, Oxford and Starkville protect city employees only; a visitor's practical exposure therefore varies sharply by which city they are in.

Public opinion in the state has moved over time. A 2019 PRRI poll found 68% of Mississippians favored laws protecting gay, lesbian, bisexual and transgender people from discrimination in jobs, housing and public accommodations, with 23% opposed, and by 2024 PRRI reported support for a statewide anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation and gender identity at 67%. The same source notes that compared to national averages Mississippi tends to show lower support for same-sex marriage and transgender rights, though opinion gaps have narrowed, with younger residents showing significantly higher support than older residents.

Several federal measures bearing on trans visitors have been blocked or enjoined in court, so the operative position on any given measure should be checked before travel.

Clayton County (15 June 2020) prohibits employment discrimination based on gender identity. Jackson, Clarksdale, Holly Springs and Magnolia ban gender-identity discrimination in employment, housing and public accommodations, while Hattiesburg, Oxford and Starkville protect city employees only. The 1994 state hate-crime statute does not include gender identity, though federal prosecution remains available under the 2009 Matthew Shepard and James Byrd Jr. Act. The Religious Liberty Accommodations Act (HB 1523), effective after the Fifth Circuit lifted an injunction on 23 June 2017, protects individuals, religious organizations and some businesses acting on beliefs that gender is determined at birth by anatomy and genetics.

Same-sex marriage has been recognized since 26 June 2015 under Obergefell v. Hodges, overriding the 1996 executive order, 1997 statutory ban and 2004 constitutional Amendment 1 approved by 86.01% of voters, though those bans remain unrepealed and Attorney General Jim Hood on 29 June 2015 directed clerks to comply or face lawsuits after initial resistance. Mississippi's sodomy statute originating in 1839, with up to ten years' imprisonment, remains on the books unenforceable since Lawrence v. Texas (2003), and persons convicted before 2003 are still required to register as sex offenders under the 1995 registration law, prompting a 2016 federal lawsuit by five residents and $400,000 in taxpayer legal fees reported in 2023.

Mississippi maintains HIV criminalization making failure to disclose HIV-positive status to a sexual partner a felony even without transmission, with at least 43 arrests for HIV-related offenses between 2004 and 2021 per a 2024 Williams Institute report.

The 6.6 per 100,000 annual killings figure for Mississippi is adjusted for undercounting by the source analysis, and the adjustment method is not detailed in the inventory; the comparison to the 6.0 per 100,000 general-population homicide rate is the source's own printed comparison line, not a like-for-like calculation.

Whether the March 2026 Mississippi law prohibiting driver's licence markers not reflecting sex assigned at birth has been challenged in court, and its current enforceable scope, is not sourced in the inventory and remains unresolved.

The inventory does not document any Mississippi-specific litigation challenging the federal passport or visa sex-marker restrictions, nor any state-level response to Executive Order 14168; the ACLU suit against the State Department is a federal action of general application.

Mississippi-specific enforcement data on the federal internal visa marking for trans athletes, and on Transportation Security Administration secondary screening outcomes for trans travellers at Mississippi airports, is not sourced in the inventory.
